title: Deterministic Verification with a Single‑Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: A Paired Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We report a sealed, preregistered paired experiment that measured the marginal verifier-detected effect of interposing a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation call per intent reused for both baseline and guarded episodes) we generated one candidate per natural‑language intent with gpt-5-mini for N_pairs = 250 and evaluated two episodes per intent: baseline (accept candidate) and guarded (deterministic validator; if failing, permit at most one automated repair). Execution completed 500 episodes with model_calls_used = 251. Observed outcomes: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); contingency n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp] (paired-bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The single discordant pair was converted to pass by the sole permitted automated repair. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the registered evidence bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated as intent‑to‑configuration translators for network operations (NetOps), promising rapid authoring of device CLI sequences and intent-driven automation. However, stochastic generation exposes operational risk: syntax deviations, incorrect command ordering, local‑policy violations, and vendor‑specific CLI subtleties can produce unsafe or non‑functional device changes. Prior empirical and survey work documents LLM feasibility for draft configurations while emphasizing the continuing need for deterministic verification or human oversight [1], [2].

A common architectural mitigation is to insert a deterministic validator between generation and acceptance and to permit bounded automated repair where mechanically verifiable defects are detected — a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pattern. Deterministic validators reliably detect many syntactic and local‑policy errors (ordering, required‑sequence violations, forbidden field modifications) while remaining agnostic to dynamic protocol behavior or cross‑device emergent effects [3], [4]. Prior work in code and configuration domains shows verifier‑guided repair can increase correction of mechanically checkable defects, but general semantic correctness and operational safety remain challenging [5], [6].

This paper presents a preregistered, artifact‑backed paired experiment that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic validation plus a single automated repair when the same initial model candidate is reused across conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics). By design the experiment measures only the verifier‑and‑single‑repair marginal effect on identical model outputs rather than conflating differences introduced by independent generation calls. We executed N_pairs = 250 constrained intent tasks in a synthetic/emulation partition using a declared model (gpt-5-mini) and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). We report the exact contingency counts, bootstrap confidence interval, and exact McNemar test computed by the preregistered analysis executor.
sections.related_work:
Two literatures motivate and contextualize this study. First, empirical NetOps work shows LLMs can produce usable draft configurations under controlled conditions but that output quality varies by prompt constraints, task specificity, and topology complexity; deterministic checks or human oversight are frequently recommended to bridge the gap to operational acceptability [1], [2]. Second, generate‑and‑verify or GVR architectures were proposed and evaluated across code and configuration domains: deterministic validators (including Batfish‑like analyses and header‑space approaches) detect forwarding and many local‑policy violations, and verifier‑guided repair can correct mechanically checkable defects while not fully solving deeper semantic or run‑time correctness questions [3], [4], [5].

Security and robustness work documents practical prompt‑injection and indirect injection threats to LLM‑integrated workflows and argues for detection, filtering, and verifier‑anchored mitigations; these concerns motivate conservative contamination and exclusion rules in our preregistration [6]. Surveys and benchmarks further document active community work on LLM evaluation for NetOps, but evaluation practices remain heterogeneous and external‑validity to production heterogeneity is open [7].

Our study differs in three preregistered, execution‑grounded ways: (i) a confirmatory paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation per intent reused for baseline and guarded evaluations); (ii) end‑to‑end provider‑call reconciliation explicitly attributing 250 shared initial generations plus 1 repair (model_calls_used = 251); and (iii) archival publication of complete validator traces, repair traces, and reconciliation artifacts to make contingency and per‑stage accounting auditable.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered with a confirmatory paired design (N_pairs = 250) and generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (probability that the guarded episode verifies where the baseline does not, minus the converse). The preregistration froze the single‑repair policy, exclusion and contamination rules, analysis tests (exact McNemar two‑sided; paired‑bootstrap percentile CIs), and a maximum model‑call budget. Execution adhered to the preregistered contract and exclusion rules (no confirmatory exclusions occurred).

Shared_initial_candidate semantics. For each intent exactly one initial LLM generation was executed; that identical candidate was evaluated under both conditions: baseline (the candidate is accepted as‑is) and guarded (the candidate is submitted to the deterministic validator; if invalid, permit at most one automated repair and re‑validate). Under these semantics only downstream validation and permitted repair can create a paired outcome difference. Provider‑call reconciliation records hosted_model_call_event_count = 251 (250 shared initial generations + 1 repair), as recorded in the archived deterministic_reconciliation artifact.

Task bank and constraints. A deterministic task generator produced 250 constrained intent tasks. Each task payload encoded initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and a difficulty label (medium/hard/very_hard). Tasks exercised workflow constraints (make‑before‑break uplink switchover, paired‑link atomic MTU changes, safe access transfer patterns) and enforced protected interfaces that must not be modified. These constraints intentionally reduce ambiguity and aim to operationalize intent‑satisfaction as a deterministic verifier judgment.

Guarded pipeline, validator, and repair. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The validator parsed CLI sequences, computed parsed_command_count, checked required_sequence ordering and workflow constraints, and compared the computed final_state snapshot to the task's expected_final_state. Validator outputs included normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, and a boolean valid flag. Repair templates were deterministic and constrained to syntactic and ordering fixes (reordering commands to match required_sequence, splitting combined commands, correcting token‑order errors). Crucially, the design permitted at most one automated repair call per episode; no multi‑iteration repair or human escalation was allowed.

Inclusion, contamination, and missingness handling. Preregistered exclusion rules removed items that deterministically prevented verification (vendor‑parser failures) or contained credential‑like tokens or denylist hits. Contamination detectors flagged instruction‑like embedded tokens and private‑address artifacts. In the confirmatory execution no episodes were excluded or flagged: complete_pair_count = 250 and contamination_summary shows zero flagged episodes. Analysis treated deterministic verifier runtime errors, if any, per the preregistered missingness plan; none occurred in this run.

Analysis procedures. The preregistered primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1. Primary inference reports the exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant counts and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the guarded − baseline paired difference with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). All analysis inputs and outputs (contingency counts, bootstrap parameters, p‑values) are preserved in the archived analysis artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution and reconciliation. Execution completed the preregistered confirmatory partition with planned_episode_count = 500, completed_episode_count = 500, complete_pair_count = 250, and model_calls_used = 251. The deterministic reconciliation artifact records hosted_model_call_event_count = 251 with stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 250 and repair = 1.

Primary binary outcomes and contingency. Validator‑scored successes were baseline_success_count = 249 (baseline_success_rate = 0.996) and guarded_success_count = 250 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The observed paired contingency is n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The single discordant pair (baseline failed, guarded passed) corresponds to the sole exercised automated repair; the observed repair‑conversion rate in the confirmatory partition is 1/250 = 0.004 (0.4%). Representative per‑episode validator traces for passing episodes show parsed_command_count equal to required_command_count for many tasks (examples archived in per‑task scoring artifacts).

Statistical inference and uncertainty. The exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant counts (n10 = 1, n01 = 0) returned p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval for the guarded − baseline paired difference (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.012] (0 – 1.2 percentage points). These values are taken directly from the preregistered analysis outputs.

Diagnostics and repair exercise. Validator traces record validation_before and validation_after snapshots, normalized configurations, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and violation lists (empty for passing episodes). Only one repair was generated and applied; its repair trace and the guarded scoring artifact for that pair show the repaired candidate satisfied the deterministic validation checks that the baseline candidate failed. No other repairs were necessary in the confirmatory partition. Missingness and exclusions: none — complete_pairs = 250 and all missingness counts = 0.
sections.discussion:
Interpreting the near‑null marginal verifier effect. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics and this constrained synthetic/emulation partition, the marginal verifier‑detected benefit of inserting a deterministic validator plus a single automated repair was small: initial gpt-5-mini candidates satisfied the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases and the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate via the permitted repair. The paired‑bootstrap CI upper bound (1.2 percentage points) provides an empirical bound on the maximum verifier‑detected improvement for this pipeline and task scope.

Artifact‑grounded factors explaining the small observed gain. The preregistered execution and archived artifacts identify three grounded contributors: (1) constrained task encoding — allowed_touched_fields and explicit required_sequence reduced ambiguity and favored well‑formed CLI outputs; (2) the declared model (gpt-5-mini) consistently produced syntactically well‑formed sequences under these constrained prompts; and (3) the deterministic validator intentionally targeted mechanically checkable properties (syntax, ordering, final_state snapshot) and therefore could not reveal or remedy dynamic protocol behaviors or complex vendor‑specific semantics outside its encoding.

Power and design considerations. The preregistration power calculation assumed a baseline pass rate ≈ 0.90 when selecting N_pairs = 250 to detect a 15 percentage‑point absolute effect with ≈80% power. The realized baseline pass rate (0.996) is substantially higher than assumed; this reduces the chance of observing a statistically significant paired difference for small absolute improvements. Consequently, the confirmatory outcome should be interpreted as a tight empirical bound (95% CI upper = 1.2 pp) on verifier‑detected improvement under the stated pipeline and task scope, rather than evidence against the utility of validators in broader or differently scoped deployments.

Operational implications and safe deployment framing. These results do not imply validators are unnecessary. Instead they quantify the marginal verifier‑detected benefit under specific, constrained conditions: (a) tightly constrained emulation tasks and a capable LLM can produce high verifier pass rates, making incremental single‑repair gains small; (b) validators remain essential to provide deterministic guarantees on mechanically checkable properties and to defend against malformed or adversarial outputs; (c) richer validators, multi‑iteration repair policies, human escalation, or external dynamic tests (live reachability or forwarding checks) could materially change measured operational benefits; and (d) production heterogeneity and adaptive adversaries remain untested here and could increase the marginal utility of guardrails.

Failure modes, diagnostics, and auditability. The dominant failure mode observed was command ordering or token‑sequence mismatches amenable to a deterministic template repair; vendor‑specific semantic mismatches or cross‑device emergent errors were not observed in this controlled task bank. All per‑episode validator traces, repair traces, and reconciliation artifacts are archived to support audit and follow‑up analyses.

Limitations and threats to external validity. The confirmatory scope is limited to the synthetic/emulation partition and a single declared model and validator implementation; preregistered community and production‑like partitions were not executed in this run. The deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties but not live protocol‑level correctness. Only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design. Adversarial and retrieval‑based attacks and large‑scale production heterogeneity were not exercised. These limitations restrict generalization and motivate broader follow‑up studies.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the verifier‑detected marginal benefit of deterministic validation plus one permitted automated repair on identical LLM‑generated configuration candidates. In N_pairs = 250 constrained synthetic intent tasks, initial gpt-5-mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases; the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate via the lone permitted repair. Observed paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). These results bound the verifier‑detected marginal improvement for the studied pipeline and task scope but do not settle broader operational, adversarial, multi‑model, or multi‑iteration repair questions.

References
[1] C. Wang et al., “NetConfEval: Can LLMs Facilitate Network Configuration?,” in Proc. ACM, 2024. 
[2] R. Kamoi et al., “When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self‑Correction of LLMs,” TACL, 2024. 
[3] R. Mondal, A. Tang, R. Beckett, T. Millstein, and G. Varghese, “What do LLMs need to Synthesize Correct Router Configurations?,” in Proc. ACM, 2023, doi: 10.1145/3626111.3628194. 
[4] M. Brown et al., “Lessons from the evolution of the Batfish configuration analysis tool,” in Proc. ACM, 2024, doi: 10.1145/3603269.3604866. 
[5] R. Cadenas, “Convergent Correctness in Stochastic Code Generation: A Generate‑Verify‑Repair Architecture for Deterministic Validation of Autonomous AI Coding Agents in Regulated Environments,” SSRN, 2026, doi: 10.2139/ssrn.6754899. 
[6] K. Greshake et al., “Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real‑World LLM‑Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection,” in Proc. ACM, 2024, doi: 10.1145/3605764.3623985. 
[7] F. Li et al., “PreConfig: A Pretrained Model for Automating Network Configuration,” arXiv:2403.09369, 2024.

disclosure_statement:
Human role and autonomy boundary: After an autonomy lock required by the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track, the autonomous system performed literature search, study selection, preregistration freeze, prompt preservation, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, analysis, drafting, peer‑review, revision, and finalization without manual human editing of technical content. A human Research Director selected the broad topic family and performed pre‑lock infrastructure development only; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.

Declared components and accounting: declared model = gpt-5-mini; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution used a guarded generate–verify–repair flow permitting at most one automated repair per episode. Provider‑call reconciliation records model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair) with per‑stage counts recorded in the archived reconciliation artifact.

Preregistration and immutable master prompt reference: the study was preregistered under the stated study identifier and the immutable master prompt used to initiate the autonomous run is archived as provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The evidence bundle contains the archived preregistration, execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts referenced in this manuscript.
limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed and remain exploratory.

Deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax and prescribed workflow sequences) but did not measure broader semantic or behavioral correctness (protocol dynamics, emergent interactions).
Single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi-model or alternate-validator generality.
Only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi-iteration repairs or human-in-the-loop escalation were not evaluated.
Adversarial and retrieval-based attacks (adaptive prompt-injection, vendor-targeted exploit vectors) and large-scale production heterogeneity were not exercised and remain open threats.
